nodes.name: elysflowers:foxglove
nodes._guidebook_entry: This highly toxic biennial herb is native to British Columbia and was later naturalized in the northern US. It produces showy purple and pink bells that dangle in clusters from the sides of the stem. Despite it's ornamental nature, foxglove is highly fatal if consumed in excess. It contains chemicals which inhibit neurotransmission. The heart medication, digitalis is actually derived from a relative of foxglove

nodes.name: elysflowers:purple_coneflower
nodes._guidebook_entry: The purple coneflower is a common sight across the prairies and open fields of Eastern and Central North America. It's name is derived from the greek word (ἐχῖνος). Which means 'spiny one'. As it's name suggests, the cone of the purple coneflower is made from many spiky protrusions where the seed capsules grow.

nodes.name: elysflowers:california_poppy
nodes._guidebook_entry:
The state flower of California, the California poppy is native to the western seaboard of the United States. Before European settlers arrived in California, 
 It's rumoured that entire hillsides would turn bright orange due to the immense number of poppies.
 The California Poppy is very drought tolerant, and incredibly responsive to intense sunlight & heat. It can be found growing in any distributed area of grass, desert scrub, or even dry gravel.

nodes.name: elysflowers:marshmallow
nodes._guidebook_entry: Often mistaken for the gooey sugary treat of the same namesake, 'marshmellows' actually get their name from this flower. The roots of the marshmallow contain a tetriary metabolite that may act as a mild numbing agent. It was often used by Native Americans as a remedy for sore throat, cooked and sweetened with a mixture of gluten, honey, and sugar.

nodes.name: elysflowers:african_marigold
nodes._guidebook_entry: Despite it's name, this flower is actually native to the hot and humid steppes of Latin America, inhabiting a wide variety of tropical and subtropical climates

nodes.name: elysflowers:arctic_poppy
nodes._guidebook_entry: The artic poppy (unsurprisingly) is a tundra flower found throughout large stretches of the North America arctic and sub-arctic.\n It prefers to grow in well-drained dry gravels and loose soils, and has an impressive reputation for being nearly impossible to kill. \n The roots of these flowers have been found alive, extracting nutrients through solid ice!

nodes.name: elysflowers:dames_rocket
nodes._guidebook_entry: This biennial herb is a short-lived, and shade tolerant forest-dweller that can often grow as tall as a standing person! \n The dames rocket produces blooms in early to late spring, which vary in color from off white to bright pink or purple.

nodes.name: elysflowers:chamomile
nodes._guidebook_entry:
Chamomile is a common herbal additive. Emitting an alluring fresh apple-like scent, the flowerheads of chamomile are used commonly in teas and skincare products. 
 Chamomile is native to europe and the temperate regions of asia, althought it is widely naturalized through North America. It can be found in the wild in distributed open areas, on roadsides, fields, irrigation ditches, and shallow riverbanks.

nodes.name: elysflowers:rose_pogonia
nodes._guidebook_entry: Native to the cooler damp forests of the great lakes basin this showy orchid is often refered to as the 'snake-mouth' plant after the peculiar geometry of it's bloom. The American romantic era poet Henry David Thoreau once allegedly remaked that the rose pogonia '...smells exactly like a snake.'

nodes.name: elysflowers:cold_desert_phlox
nodes._guidebook_entry: This perennial herb is native to dry arid regions of the American southwest. As it's name suggests cold desert phlox can often be found among the desert scrub of temperate, to mildly cold deserts and dry grasslands.

nodes.name: elysflowers:western_bleeding_heart
nodes._guidebook_entry:
This orchid was introduced to North America from Japan. 
 It has since colonized much of the western seaboard from British Columbia all the way to southern California. 
 Prefers to grow in damp, heavily shaded areas.

nodes.name: elysflowers:siberian_chive
nodes._guidebook_entry:
This grassy herb is native to the upper stretches of the Yukon, althought it can be found as far south as Ontario.
 The siberian chive is found most commonly in the wild near mountain streams, and cool damp meadows.
 The siberan chive was registered by the Vermont State office of Fish & Wildlife as an endangered species in 2024.

nodes.name: elysflowers:evening_primrose
nodes._guidebook_entry:
The flowers open in the evening, and close by noon.
 It can be found scattered in fields, alongside roads, in irrigation ditches, and just about anywhere that gets enough light and water.

nodes.name: elysflowers:yellow_flag
nodes._guidebook_entry:
The yellow flag is recognized as an invasive species of iris in North America. Due in part to it's natural tolerance of low oxygen, and high salinity substrate. It prefers to grow in salt or freshwater marshes or along river and stream banks.
 To reproduce effectively, the seeds of the yellow flag have small air-tight chambers that allow them to float across water over long distances

nodes.name: elysflowers:desert_plume
nodes._guidebook_entry: The Desert Plume, also known as the Desert Prince's Plume is the prince of arid open deserts. They are highly drought tolerant. After their deep taproots are properly established they can survive dozens of completey rainless seasons. Interestingly, the Desert Plume might be a biological indicator of higher than normal selenieum presence in the enviorment

nodes.name: elysflowers:canada_violet
nodes._guidebook_entry:
The deep green and heart-shaped leaves of the Canada violet make ideal hosts for the larva of some small butterflies. The Canada violet is partial to the nutrient rich, old-growth, and often coniferious hardwood forests of western Canada. Where it will usually be found happily subsisting among the scrub of the forest floor.
 The leaves are edible, and make a fine addition or garish to a salad.
